..
Tonight through Saturday afternoon: A robust upper-level low 
digging down the Pac NW coastline will have some influence on 
the weather pattern across the Inland NW but conditions will 
remain dry. The main impacts will be an influx of mid and high 
clouds with overcast conditions at times. Second will be an 
increasing east to northeast pressure gradient leading to breezy
conditions starting early Saturday morning and becoming gusty 
Saturday afternoon. Sustained winds of 10-15 mph with gusts 
around 25 mph will be common across the Idaho Panhandle, West 
Plains, Palouse, and across the Columbia Basin.

Saturday evening through Sunday night: The aforementioned upper-low 
will pivot inland, driven by a 100+ kt jet over E Oregon. 
Strong divergence aloft, enhanced ascent within the left exit 
region of the jet, and positive vorticity advection will promote
surface cyclogensis over Central WA with model surface 
pressures varying between 1004-1006 mb. A warm conveyor belt of 
richer theta-e air will be pulled across E WA and wrap into the 
system resulting in a quite the fall storm system for the 
region. The track of this low has wavered some over the last few
days and even in the last 12 hours with most guidance trending 
further west and north. This has resulted in shifts in the QPF 
amounts and probabilities for moderate to heavy rainfall with 
amounts decreasing in SE WA and the ID Panhandle by 0.20-0.40 
inches and increasing over Central WA by 0.10-0.40 inches. Could
this continue to change - you bet but general 
consensus/ensemble means are trending in this direction. 

So majority of the Inland NW will receive rainfall from this system.  
Rain for the Idaho Panhandle and Eastern WA will come in form 
of several transitory waves with embedded thunderstorms at 
times. A few storms Sunday afternoon and early evening will need
to be monitored closely with the potential for sunbreaks, CAPE 
of 400-600 J/kg and effective shear of 30+ kts. This includes 
the L-C Valley, Palouse, and lower Idaho Panhandle. Rainfall for
Central WA will be more steady with varying light to moderate 
intensities. A few lightning strikes cannot be ruled out 
Saturday night into early Sunday morning but this comes with 
lower confidence. 

There is nearly a 90-100% chance for a wetting rain (0.10 inches) 
for most locations across the Inland NW. Lowest probabilities 
are across the far north Cascades between Stehekin to Conconully
which are closer to 70-80%. As for half an inch of rain (0.50 
inches) or more, percentages vary from 50% at Omak to 70-80% at 
Wenatchee and Moses Lake. Much of Eastern WA and North Idaho 
reside between 70-80%. The bigger differences come when viewing 
one inch or more and as follows:

- 15-50% for Central WA (lowest at Omak and Stehekin)
- 35-50% for Eastern WA 
- 30-50% for ID Panhandle (lowest around Bonners Ferry and Lewiston)

For the most part, the rain will be mainly beneficial for the area.  
Of most concern will be burn scars and where persistent rains 
for 12+ hours lead to swaths over an inch (Central WA) and/or 
convective cells create heavier intensities (Eastern WA and 
North Idaho). Given the recent fires across the region and areas
with steeper terrain, a hydrologic outlook has been issued to 
address the potential for these rains over burn scars. Folks 
that may be recreating in the backcountry should be prepared for
cool and wet conditions with highs in the 40-50s.

Monday through Friday: The weekend storm system will depart early 
Monday with another weak wave dropping in from the north 
Tuesday. This will keep a mention of showers mainly in the 
northern mountains with light additional precipitation. The main
sensible weather impacts will be a transition toward warmer and
drier conditions with temperatures rebounding back into the 
70s-80s.
